what_its_for: This medicine helps control blood sugar levels in adults with type 2 diabetes. It works in two ways: saxagliptin helps your body release more insulin when blood sugar is high, and metformin reduces the amount of sugar your liver makes and helps your body use insulin better. It is used along with diet and exercise to keep your blood sugar in a healthy range.
how_to_take: Take this medicine by mouth once a day with your evening meal. Swallow the tablet whole — do not crush, cut, or chew it. Taking it with food helps reduce stomach upset. If you need to take an X-ray or scan with dye (contrast material), let your doctor know right away, as you may need to temporarily stop this medicine.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your current diabetes medicines and kidney function. The typical starting dose is one tablet per day with the evening meal. The dose may be adjusted over time. Never change your dose without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if you remember with your evening meal. If you have already finished your meal or it is the next day, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the usual time with your next evening meal. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store in the bathroom. Keep this medicine in its original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Properly dispose of any unused medicine.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking large amounts of alcohol while taking this medicine, as alcohol can affect your blood sugar and increase the risk of a rare but serious condition called lactic acidosis. Avoid missing meals or eating much less than usual, as this can cause low blood sugar. Tell your doctor before starting any new medicines, supplements, or herbal products. Avoid dehydration — drink plenty of fluids, especially if you have vomiting, diarrhea, or are sweating heavily.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: muscle pain or weakness, trouble breathing, stomach pain, nausea or vomiting, feeling cold or dizzy, or unusual sleepiness — these could be signs of lactic acidosis, a rare but serious side effect. Also call your doctor if you have: signs of low blood sugar (shakiness, sweating, fast heartbeat, confusion), signs of pancreatitis (severe stomach pain that may spread to your back), painful blisters or sores on your skin, signs of a urinary tract infection (burning when urinating, frequent urination), or any allergic reaction (rash, swelling of the face or throat, trouble breathing).
when_it_works: Metformin starts working within the first few days, but it may take 1 to 2 weeks to see the full effect on your blood sugar. Saxagliptin starts working relatively quickly to help control blood sugar after meals. It usually takes a few weeks to a few months to see the full benefit. Keep taking this medicine as directed even if you feel well — diabetes often has no symptoms.
special_populations: Kidney problems: This medicine is not recommended if your kidneys are not working well. Your doctor will check your kidney function before and during treatment. Elderly patients (65 and older): Use with caution. Kidney function should be monitored closely. Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor before taking this medicine if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Breastfeeding: It is not known if this medicine passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Children: This medicine is not approved for use in patients under 18 years of age. Heart failure: Tell your doctor if you have heart failure, as saxagliptin may increase the risk of hospitalization in some patients with heart failure.
